case, detailing the potential costs, benefits and risks associated. As part of this process, the Board

8.2  Eligibility and qualification of a business case 
The business case should contain a selection criterion that includes specific requirements and service 
expectations, which enables a fair and impartial selection prior to outsourcing to a third party. The 
selection criteria must consider assessing the following (as a minimum):  
• 
The financial resources of the third party to deliver the services, 
• 
The third party’s technical resources, systems, and capacity to deliver the required services, 
• 
The human resources of the third party having relevant skills to provide the services, 
• 
The third party’s compliance plans and procedures, 
• 
The third circumstances party’s internal control framework covering risk management, 
performance standards, policies, procedures, internal audit, review and compliance arrangements, 
reporting, and monitoring processes, 
• 
An assessment of the anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing risks of the third party, 
• 
The fees to be charged by a third party. 
9. Due Diligence 
The due diligence should be conducted before any final decision is made to determine whether to 
outsource a material activity or not. This should address all material factors that would impact the 
potential Third party’s ability to perform the business activity.  
The due diligence process should, as a minimum, assess the financial ability, technical ability, and 
capacity of the third party to deliver, including in stressful situations, the required services.

PURPOSE

The purpose of this Directive is to, under sections 4(4) of the Long-term Insurance
Act No. 52 of 1998 and the Short-term Insurance Act No. 53 of 1998 (‘the Acts”),
tead with sections 9(3}(b){i) and sections 12(1)(c) of the Acts, respectively, direct
long-term and short-term insurers (“insurers”) to comply with the requirements set
out in this Directive when outsourcing an aspect of their long-term or short-term
insurance business {“insurance business”) to another person.

BACKGROUND

Outsourcing may materially increase risk to insurers or materially adversely affect
their ability to manage risks and meet regulatory obligations.

International standards’ require an appropriate legislative framework that mitigates
the potential adverse effect referred to in paragraph 2.1.

APPLICATION AND SCOPE OF DIRECTIVE

This Directive applies to all insurers (including, subject to paragraph 3.6,
reinsurers).

The evaluation process should include an assessment of the third party’s control framework, covering 
performance standards, policies, procedures, compliance, reporting, and monitoring processes.  
The due diligence should also address other issues, such as business strategy, reputation, 
experience with the proposed outsourced function, reliance on and performance of external third 
party, insurance coverage, business continuity management, and potential conflict of interest where 
the third party is related to ABC or has arrangements with competitors.

Overseas Outsourcing 
In addition to the general due diligence process outlined above, in assessing whether to approve an 
application to offshore a Material Outsourcing Arrangement, would expect to consider the risks which 
could arise from overseas Outsourcing, including:  
• 
Country risk - the risk that overseas economic, political, and/or social events will impact the ability 
of the overseas third party to continue to provide an outsourced service to ABC.  
• 
Compliance (legal) risk - the risk that overseas outsourcing arrangements will impact ABC’s ability 
to comply with relevant Saudi Arabia and overseas laws and regulations (including accounting 
practices). 
• 
Contractual risk - the risk that ABC’s ability to enforce the overseas outsourcing agreement may 
be partly or completely hindered. 
• 
Access risk - the risk that the ability of ABC to obtain information and to retain records may be 
partly or completely hindered. This risk also refers to the potential difficulties or inability of ABC to 
access the third party and the material function activity being conducted. 
• 
Counterparty risk - the risk arising from the third party’s failure to meet the terms of any contract 
with ABC or to otherwise perform as agreed. 
• 
Brand risk – the risk arising from the third party’s failure to protect or respond to the damage done 
to ABC’s reputation including through contagion. 
• 
Security risk – the risk arising from the third party’s failure to have secure systems to protect their 
held data against cyberattacks or internal system breaches.  
These and other additional risks should be specifically addressed during the preparation of a business 
case when conducting the due diligence and during contract negotiations. Where ABC approves the 
overseas material outsourcing arrangement, these risks should also be considered when conducting 
the ongoing monitoring and control of that Material Outsourcing Arrangement. Specific risk 
management expertise is required when assessing, monitoring, and controlling material business 
activities outsourced to service providers conducting the activities outside Saudi Arabia.

• 
Overall risk profile and appetite; and  
• 
Systems and controls.

practices). 
• 
Contractual risk - the risk that ABC’s ability to enforce the overseas outsourcing agreement may 
be partly or completely hindered. 
•

partly or completely hindered. This risk also refers to the potential difficulties or inability of ABC to 
access the third party and the material function activity being conducted. 
• 
Counterparty risk - the risk arising from the third party’s failure to meet the terms of any contract 
with ABC or to otherwise perform as agreed.
